Harper's Magazine. Founded in 1850, it is one of the oldest continuously published American magazines. In its early years, Harper's was revolutionary. It achieved mass circulation exceeding 200,000 copies, unprecedented for a literary magazine, and it serialized Charles Dickens' works. The magazine features The Easy Chair, a column of satirical essays dating back to 1851, making it one of journalism's longest-running features. Throughout its history, Harper's has published major investigative journalism and social commentary, famous for exposing political corruption and social injustice. The editorial voice emphasized literary quality, progressive social reform, and intellectual engagement with American issues. Circulation declined in the twentieth century but the magazine maintained its prestige as a journal of serious non-fiction and criticism. It became known for Harper's Index, a monthly collection of statistics and facts illustrating trends in American culture and politics, and it pioneered the magazine format for serious literary content.
